title: Kubernetes Workloads
subtitle: Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs and healthy Pods
description: Pick the right controller for each workload, roll out changes safely, run batch jobs and tell Kubernetes how healthy and how large your containers are.
outcomes: Choose between Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet and Job
Roll out and roll back releases with controlled strategy
Configure probes and resources to keep Pods stable

lessons.title: Deployments and ReplicaSets
lessons.summary: Run stateless apps declaratively: replicas, rolling updates, rollback and the knobs that control rollout speed.
objectives: Explain how a Deployment manages ReplicaSets and Pods
Scale and update a Deployment and watch the rollout
Tune maxSurge and maxUnavailable and roll back a bad release

sections.title: Deployment, ReplicaSet, Pod
sections.body:
A **Deployment** declares the desired state of a stateless app. It creates a **ReplicaSet**, which keeps the requested number of identical Pods running. You almost never create ReplicaSets directly: when the Pod template changes, the Deployment creates a *new* ReplicaSet and gradually shifts Pods from the old one to the new one.

Old ReplicaSets are kept (scaled to 0) so you can roll back. `revisionHistoryLimit` (default 10) controls how many are retained.

sections.caption: Click a box to see what it does.

sections.title: What this example is
sections.body: `deployment.yaml` is a manifest: a YAML file that describes the Deployment we want, and you create it with `kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml`. We show it first because every later command in this lesson works on this `web` Deployment. Look at `replicas: 3` (how many Pods), `selector.matchLabels` and the template `labels` (they must match), the `strategy` block with `maxSurge: 1` and `maxUnavailable: 0`, and `image: nginx:1.27`.

sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: nginx:1.27
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
sections.title: deployment.yaml
sections.note: `spec.selector` must match the template labels and is immutable after creation.

sections.title: Rolling update parameters
head: Field
Meaning
Default
rows: Extra Pods allowed above `replicas` during the update (number or %)
Pods that may be unavailable during the update
Kill all old Pods, then start new ones (downtime)

sections.title: Why maxUnavailable: 0 matters
sections.body: With `maxSurge: 1` and `maxUnavailable: 0`, Kubernetes starts one new Pod, waits for it to become **Ready**, and only then terminates an old one. Capacity never drops, but the rollout is only as safe as your readiness probe: without one, a Pod counts as ready the moment its container starts.

sections.title: What this example is
sections.body: The next block is a list of `kubectl` commands you type in a terminal, in order, to run and change the `web` Deployment from `deployment.yaml`. It shows the everyday life of a release: create it, scale it to 5 Pods, update the image to `nginx:1.28`, watch the rollout, then undo or pause it. Pay attention to `kubectl set image` (starts a rolling update) and `kubectl rollout undo` (goes back to the previous version); the output below each command shows what Kubernetes answers.

kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl scale deployment/web --replicas=5
kubectl set image deployment/web web=nginx:1.28
kubectl rollout status deployment/web
kubectl rollout history deployment/web
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web --to-revision=1
kubectl rollout pause deployment/web

sections.title: What this example is
sections.body: These are read-only `kubectl` commands that let you look at what the Deployment created, without changing anything. We run them after the rollout to see the three layers: the Deployment (`get deploy`), its ReplicaSets (`get rs`) and the Pods (`get pods -o wide`). In the output, compare the READY, UP-TO-DATE and AVAILABLE columns, and notice that an old and a new ReplicaSet can exist side by side.

kubectl get rs -l app=web
kubectl get pods -l app=web -o wide
kubectl describe deploy web
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -6

items.title: Before: 5 old Pods
items.body: `web-5d8c7f6b9d` has 5/5 Pods on nginx:1.27, `web-7c4b9f8d6b` does not exist yet.

items.title: Surge: 1 new Pod
items.body: With maxSurge 1 and maxUnavailable 0 the new ReplicaSet scales to 1. Total Pods: 6 (5 old + 1 new).

items.title: New Pod becomes Ready
items.body: Only now is one old Pod removed: old 4, new 1. Capacity never drops below 5.

items.title: Repeat
items.body: Old 4/new 1, then old 3/new 2 ... each step waits for readiness.

items.title: After: 5 new Pods
items.body: `web-7c4b9f8d6b` 5/5 on nginx:1.28, `web-5d8c7f6b9d` scaled to 0 and kept for rollback.

sections.title: What this example is
sections.body: This is a second version of the `web` Deployment manifest, applied with `kubectl apply -f`, that adds the fields which control how a rollout behaves. It is here so you can see where the tuning knobs live. Look at `maxSurge: 25%` and `maxUnavailable: 25%` (rollout speed), `minReadySeconds` and `progressDeadlineSeconds` (how long a new Pod must be healthy and when a rollout counts as failed), `revisionHistoryLimit` (how many old ReplicaSets are kept for rollback) and the `change-cause` annotation.

sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/change-cause: "bump nginx to 1.28"
spec:
  replicas: 5
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
  minReadySeconds: 5
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 300
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: nginx:1.28
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
sections.title: Sample: rollout tuning fields
sections.note: With 5 replicas, 25% surge rounds up to 2 extra Pods and 25% unavailable rounds down to 1. `change-cause` fills the CHANGE-CAUSE column of rollout history.

sections.title: Record why you changed things
sections.body: Use `kubectl annotate deployment/web kubernetes.io/change-cause="upgrade to nginx 1.28"` so `rollout history` shows a meaningful CHANGE-CAUSE column.

sections.title: What this example is
sections.body: This is sample terminal output (not a file you run) from `kubectl get deploy,rs` and `kubectl get pods`, captured at three moments: before, during and after a rollout with a broken image tag. We show it so you recognise what a bad release looks like and why it is safe. Follow the READY and UP-TO-DATE numbers: the new Pod stays `0/1 ImagePullBackOff` while the 5 old Pods stay available, and the last line tells you the fix, `kubectl rollout undo`.

sections.code:
# Before (kubectl get deploy,rs)
web   5/5   5   5    deploy: nginx:1.27
web-5d8c7f6b9d   5 5 5

# Mid-rollout (maxSurge 1, maxUnavailable 0)
web   5/5   2   5
web-5d8c7f6b9d   4 4 4
web-7c4b9f8d6b   1 1 1

# Failed rollout (bad image tag nginx:9.9)
NAME   READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
web    5/5     1            5           20m
web-7c4b9f8d6b-abcde   0/1   ImagePullBackOff   0   2m
# old Pods keep serving; fix with: kubectl rollout undo deployment/web
sections.title: Sample: what you see during a bad rollout
sections.note: Because maxUnavailable is 0, a broken new version never takes down the working Pods.

exercises.title: Scale and observe
exercises.prompt: Create a Deployment with 2 replicas of nginx, then scale to 4 and list the ReplicaSet.
exercises.expected: After `kubectl scale deployment/web --replicas=4`, `kubectl get rs` shows DESIRED 4 and READY 4.
exercises.solution: kubectl scale deployment/web --replicas=4 && kubectl get rs -l app=web

exercises.title: Break and roll back
exercises.prompt: Deploy a non-existent image tag, watch it stall, then roll back.
exercises.expected: New Pods show ErrImagePull/ImagePullBackOff while old Pods keep serving; `kubectl rollout undo deployment/web` restores a healthy state.
exercises.hint: The container name is `nginx` when created with `kubectl create deployment`.
exercises.solution: kubectl rollout status deployment/web --timeout=30s; kubectl rollout undo deployment/web

questions.question: What creates the Pods in a Deployment?
options: A ReplicaSet owned by the Deployment
questions.explain: The Deployment controller manages ReplicaSets, and each ReplicaSet creates its Pods.

questions.question: Which settings guarantee no loss of serving capacity during a rolling update?
questions.explain: Surging first and allowing zero unavailable means new Pods become Ready before old ones are removed.

questions.question: What does `kubectl rollout undo deployment/web` do?
options: Reverts the Pod template to the previous revision
questions.explain: It restores the previous ReplicaSet's template, creating a new rollout.

questions.question: Why can a rollout with no readiness probe be dangerous?
options: Pods are considered ready as soon as the container starts
questions.explain: Without readiness, traffic and the rollout advance to Pods that may not be able to serve yet.

lessons.title: StatefulSets
lessons.summary: Run stateful apps with stable network identity and per-Pod persistent storage.
objectives: Explain what a StatefulSet guarantees that a Deployment does not
Define a headless Service and volumeClaimTemplates
Predict ordering and storage behaviour on scale and delete

sections.title: Stable identity
sections.body:
A **StatefulSet** gives each Pod a sticky identity: a predictable name (`db-0`, `db-1`, ...), a stable DNS name, and its own PersistentVolumeClaim. If `db-1` is rescheduled it comes back as `db-1` and reattaches to the same volume.

By default Pods are created in order (0, 1, 2) and terminated in reverse order. Use `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` if your app does not need ordering.

sections.caption: Click a box to see what it does.

sections.title: What this example is
sections.body: `statefulset.yaml` is a manifest with two objects separated by `---`: a headless Service named `db` and a StatefulSet named `db`; you create both with `kubectl apply -f statefulset.yaml`. We show it as the standard recipe for running a database with stable identity and its own disk. Look at `clusterIP: None` (makes the Service headless), `serviceName: db` (links the StatefulSet to it), `replicas: 3`, and `volumeClaimTemplates` at the bottom, which gives every Pod its own storage.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: db
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: db
  ports:
    - port: 5432
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: db
spec:
  serviceName: db
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: db
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: postgres:16
          env:
            - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
              value: example
            - name: PGDATA
              value: /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 5Gi
sections.title: statefulset.yaml
sections.note: `clusterIP: None` makes the Service headless: DNS returns individual Pod IPs instead of one virtual IP. Use a Secret for the password in real clusters.

sections.title: DNS names
sections.body: A headless Service gives each Pod a DNS record of the form `<pod>.<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`, for example `db-0.db.default.svc.cluster.local`. Clients such as replicas of a database use these names to find a specific primary or peer.

sections.title: PVCs are not deleted automatically
sections.body: Deleting or scaling down a StatefulSet does **not** delete the PVCs created from `volumeClaimTemplates`, protecting your data. Delete them explicitly, or set `persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy` to opt in to automatic cleanup.

sections.title: What this example is
sections.body: These `kubectl` commands show how the Pods of the `db` StatefulSet behave after you applied `statefulset.yaml`. We list the Pods and their PVCs, scale down, ask a Pod for its hostname, and delete one Pod on purpose. In the output look at the predictable names `db-0`, `db-1`, `db-2` and notice that a deleted Pod comes back with the same name and the same PVC.

sections.code:
kubectl get sts,pods -l app=db
kubectl get pvc
kubectl scale sts/db --replicas=2
kubectl exec db-0 -- hostname
kubectl delete pod db-1
kubectl get pod db-1 -w

sections.title: What this example is
sections.body: These commands check that each Pod can be reached by its own DNS name and then clean up leftover storage. The first one starts a temporary busybox Pod that runs `nslookup db-0.db`, the second shows the StatefulSet, and the last deletes the PVC `data-db-2` that stayed behind after scaling down. In the output, look at the `Address` line: it is the IP of the single Pod `db-0`, not a shared virtual IP.

kubectl run -it --rm dns --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- nslookup db-0.db
kubectl get sts db -o wide
kubectl delete pvc data-db-2

sections.title: Rolling update sample
sections.body: StatefulSet updates go in reverse ordinal order: `db-2`, then `db-1`, then `db-0`, waiting for each to be Ready. Set `updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.partition: 2` to update only Pods with ordinal >= 2 (a canary).

sections.title: What this example is
sections.body: This is a changed version of the `db` StatefulSet from `statefulset.yaml`, applied with `kubectl apply -f`, that demonstrates a canary update. We use it to update only one Pod first and keep the others on the old version. The key line is `rollingUpdate.partition: 2`: only Pods with an ordinal of 2 or higher (so just `db-2`) get the new image `postgres:16.4`. The `persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy` lines say that PVCs are kept (`Retain`) on delete or scale-down.

sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: db
spec:
  serviceName: db
  replicas: 3
  podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      partition: 2
  persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy:
    whenDeleted: Retain
    whenScaled: Retain
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: db
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: postgres:16.4
          env:
            - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
              value: example
            - name: PGDATA
              value: /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 5Gi
sections.title: Sample: canary update with partition
sections.note: Only db-2 gets postgres:16.4; lower the partition to 0 to roll out to the rest. Apply the headless Service from the first example too.

questions.question: Which resource is required for stable per-Pod DNS names?
questions.explain: serviceName must reference a headless Service.

questions.question: What happens to PVCs when you scale a StatefulSet down?
questions.explain: Retention protects data; cleanup is manual unless a retention policy is set.

questions.question: In what order are Pods terminated with OrderedReady?
questions.explain: Highest ordinal first, so db-2 stops before db-1.

questions.question: Why use volumeClaimTemplates instead of one shared PVC?
options: Each Pod gets its own volume
questions.explain: The template creates a separate PVC per replica.

lessons.title: DaemonSets
lessons.summary: Run one Pod per node for agents such as log shippers, monitors and network plugins.
objectives: Describe when a DaemonSet is the right controller
Restrict a DaemonSet with nodeSelector and tolerations

sections.title: One Pod per node
sections.body: A **DaemonSet** ensures a copy of a Pod runs on every (or selected) node. When a node joins, the Pod is added; when it leaves, the Pod is garbage collected. Typical uses are log collectors (Fluent Bit), node metrics exporters, CNI plugins and storage drivers.

sections.title: What this example is
sections.body: This is a manifest for a DaemonSet called `node-exporter`, created with `kubectl apply -f`; it runs a monitoring agent that exposes metrics from every node. It is the typical DaemonSet use case, so we show it right after the idea of one Pod per node. Look at what is missing (there is no `replicas`, because the node count decides), the `tolerations` entry that lets it also run on control-plane nodes, `hostPort: 9100`, and `updateStrategy` with `maxUnavailable: 1`.

sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: node-exporter
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: node-exporter
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: node-exporter
    spec:
      tolerations:
        - key: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane
          operator: Exists
          effect: NoSchedule
      containers:
        - name: exporter
          image: quay.io/prometheus/node-exporter:v1.8.2
          ports:
            - containerPort: 9100
              hostPort: 9100
sections.note: The toleration lets the Pod run on control-plane nodes, which are tainted by default.

sections.title: Targeting nodes
sections.body: Add `nodeSelector` or `nodeAffinity` in the Pod template to run only on matching nodes, for example GPU nodes. Taints repel Pods; a DaemonSet must tolerate a node's taints to be scheduled there.

sections.title: Updates
sections.body: `RollingUpdate` replaces Pods node by node, `maxUnavailable` at a time. `OnDelete` only recreates a Pod after you delete it manually, giving full control for sensitive agents.

sections.title: What this example is
sections.body: These are `kubectl` commands for checking and updating the `node-exporter` DaemonSet. We list DaemonSets in the `kube-system` namespace, see on which nodes the Pods run (`-o wide` adds a NODE column), wait for a rollout to finish, and change the image. Run them after applying the manifest above, and check that you get exactly one Pod per node.

sections.code:
kubectl get ds -n kube-system
kubectl get pods -o wide -l app=node-exporter
kubectl rollout status ds/node-exporter
kubectl set image ds/node-exporter exporter=quay.io/prometheus/node-exporter:v1.8.2
sections.output:
$ kubectl get ds -n kube-system

sections.title: What this example is
sections.body: This is another DaemonSet manifest, named `log-agent`, applied with `kubectl apply -f`. It shows how to run the Pod only on some nodes instead of all of them. Look at `nodeSelector: disktype: ssd`: only nodes labelled `disktype=ssd` get a Pod. Also see the `hostPath` volume, which lets the agent read the node's own `/var/log`, something a normal Deployment rarely needs.

sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: log-agent
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: log-agent
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: log-agent
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        disktype: ssd
      containers:
        - name: agent
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c", "tail -F /var/log/syslog"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: varlog
              mountPath: /var/log
              readOnly: true
      volumes:
        - name: varlog
          hostPath:
            path: /var/log

lessons.title: Jobs and CronJobs
lessons.summary: Run work to completion once or on a schedule, with retries, parallelism and overlap control.
objectives: Configure completions, parallelism and backoffLimit on a Job
Write a CronJob schedule and choose a concurrencyPolicy

sections.title: Jobs run to completion
sections.body:
A **Job** creates Pods and retries them until a number of them succeed. Unlike a Deployment, a successful Pod is not restarted. Pods in a Job must use `restartPolicy: OnFailure` or `Never`.

`completions` is how many successful Pods are needed, `parallelism` how many run at once, and `backoffLimit` (default 6) how many failures are tolerated before the Job is marked Failed, with exponential back-off between retries.

sections.caption: Click a box to see what it does.

sections.title: What this example is
sections.body: This is a manifest for a Job called `report`, created with `kubectl apply -f job.yaml`; it runs a small task until it succeeds instead of running forever. We show it as the basic shape of a batch Job. Look at `completions: 5` (five successful Pods are needed), `parallelism: 2` (two run at once), `backoffLimit: 3` (retries before giving up), `restartPolicy: Never`, and `ttlSecondsAfterFinished` (automatic cleanup).

sections.code:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: report
spec:
  completions: 5
  parallelism: 2
  backoffLimit: 3
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 600
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 3600
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: report
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c", "echo generating report; sleep 5"]

sections.title: CronJobs
sections.body: A **CronJob** creates Jobs on a cron schedule (`minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week`). `concurrencyPolicy` decides what happens if the previous run is still going: `Allow` (default), `Forbid` (skip the new run) or `Replace` (cancel the old one). `startingDeadlineSeconds` limits how late a missed run may start.

sections.title: What this example is
sections.body: This is a manifest for a CronJob called `nightly-backup`, applied with `kubectl apply -f`; it creates a new Job on a schedule. It is here because most real batch work is repeated. Read `schedule: "0 2 * * *"` (every day at 02:00), `timeZone`, `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid` (skip a run if the last one is still going), the two history limits, and `jobTemplate`, which is simply a Job spec nested inside.

sections.code:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: nightly-backup
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  timeZone: "Europe/Berlin"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 1
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 2
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          containers:
            - name: backup
              image: busybox:1.36
              command: ["sh", "-c", "echo backing up"]

sections.title: Make jobs idempotent
sections.body: A CronJob may rarely run a task twice or skip a run. Design tasks so repeating them is harmless.

sections.title: What this example is
sections.body: These `kubectl` commands create and manage Jobs without writing a YAML file. We create a one-off Job, list it, read its logs, trigger the CronJob `nightly-backup` by hand with `--from=cronjob/...`, and pause its schedule with `suspend: true`. Use them for quick tests and for running a backup now; the manual run is the part to remember.

sections.code:
kubectl create job once --image=busybox -- echo hello
kubectl get jobs
kubectl logs job/once
kubectl create job manual-run --from=cronjob/nightly-backup
kubectl patch cronjob nightly-backup -p '{"spec":{"suspend":true}}'

sections.title: What this example is
sections.body: This is a Job manifest named `flaky`, applied with `kubectl apply -f`, whose container runs `exit 1`, so it fails on purpose. We use it to see what Kubernetes does with a task that never succeeds. Look at `backoffLimit: 2` (after that many retries the Job is marked Failed) and `restartPolicy: Never` (each retry is a new Pod, so you can read the logs of every failed attempt).

sections.code:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: flaky
spec:
  backoffLimit: 2
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: task
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c", "echo trying; exit 1"]
sections.title: Sample: a failing Job

$ kubectl get jobs flaky

$ kubectl describe job flaky | tail -4
Events:

sections.note: Failed Pods are kept so you can read their logs until the Job is deleted.

lessons.title: Health probes and resource requests/limits
lessons.summary: Teach Kubernetes when your app is alive, ready and how much CPU and memory it needs.
objectives: Choose between liveness, readiness and startup probes
Set requests and limits and derive the QoS class

sections.title: Three probes, three jobs
sections.body:
**Startup** probe: has the app finished booting? Other probes are disabled until it passes. **Readiness** probe: should this Pod receive traffic? Failure removes it from Service endpoints but does not restart it. **Liveness** probe: is the process stuck? Failure makes the kubelet restart the container.

Probes can be `httpGet`, `tcpSocket`, `exec` or `grpc`.

sections.title: What this example is
sections.body: This is only a fragment of a Pod spec (the `containers:` part of a manifest, not a full file) showing all three probes and the resources of one container named `api`. It sits here to show how the probes from the previous text are written. Look at `startupProbe` (allows up to 30 x 2s to boot), `readinessProbe` on `/ready` (controls traffic), `livenessProbe` on `/healthz` (restarts the container after 3 failures), and `requests` and `limits` under `resources`.

sections.code:
containers:
  - name: api
    image: myorg/api:2.1
    startupProbe:
      httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}
      failureThreshold: 30
      periodSeconds: 2
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet: {path: /ready, port: 8080}
      periodSeconds: 5
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
    resources:
      requests: {cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi}
      limits: {memory: 512Mi}
sections.note: This startup probe allows up to 60 seconds to boot.

sections.title: Do not check dependencies in liveness
sections.body: If liveness depends on a database and the database blips, every Pod restarts at once and turns a small outage into a large one. Keep liveness local; put dependency checks in readiness.

sections.title: Requests, limits and QoS
sections.body:
The scheduler places Pods using **requests**. **Limits** are enforced at runtime: exceeding a CPU limit causes throttling, exceeding the memory limit gets the container **OOMKilled** (exit code 137).

The QoS class is derived from the settings: **Guaranteed** (requests equal limits for every container's CPU and memory), **Burstable** (some request or limit set), **BestEffort** (none). Under node pressure BestEffort Pods are evicted first, then Burstable.

sections.title: QoS classes
head: Class
Condition
Eviction order
rows: requests == limits for CPU and memory, all containers
At least one request or limit set

sections.title: What this example is
sections.body: These `kubectl` commands help you find out why a Pod such as `api-7d9f` was restarted or killed. The first shows how the previous container ended (`Last State`, for example OOMKilled), the second prints its QoS class, `kubectl top pod` shows live CPU and memory use, and the last lists events for that Pod. Use them when a Pod restarts and you suspect memory limits or a failing probe.

sections.code:
kubectl describe pod api-7d9f | grep -A5 "Last State"
kubectl get pod api-7d9f -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'
kubectl top pod
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=api-7d9f
sections.output:
$ kubectl describe pod api-7d9f | grep -A5 "Last State"
    Last State:     Terminated
      Reason:       OOMKilled
      Exit Code:    137
      Started:      Thu, 13 Nov 2026 09:12:04 +0100
      Finished:     Thu, 13 Nov 2026 09:14:51 +0100
$ kubectl get pod api-7d9f -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'
Burstable
$ kubectl top pod
NAME       CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
api-7d9f   42m          187Mi
$ kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=api-7d9f
LAST SEEN   TYPE      REASON      OBJECT         MESSAGE
3m          Warning   Unhealthy   pod/api-7d9f   Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503
2m          Warning   BackOff     pod/api-7d9f   Back-off restarting failed container api in pod api-7d9f
sections.note: `Reason: OOMKilled` and `Exit Code: 137` in Last State confirm a memory-limit kill.

sections.title: What this example is
sections.body: This is a complete, working `Deployment` manifest called `api` that you can apply with `kubectl apply -f`; it puts the probes and resources into a real file instead of a fragment. We show it so you can copy a full example. Look at where `startupProbe`, `readinessProbe`, `livenessProbe` and `resources` sit inside the container, and check that the probe ports match the `containerPort`.

sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: nginx:1.27
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          startupProbe:
            httpGet: {path: /, port: 80}
            failureThreshold: 30
            periodSeconds: 2
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: {path: /, port: 80}
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: {path: /, port: 80}
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi}
            limits: {memory: 512Mi}

sections.body: This is sample output of `kubectl describe pod` for a Pod whose liveness probe keeps failing; it is text you read, not a file you apply. We show it so you can recognise this problem in real life. Look at `Restart Count: 4`, `Ready: False`, `Last State: Terminated`, and the Events at the bottom: `Liveness probe failed` followed by `Killing`, which means the kubelet is restarting the container.
